findings.rule: Brief A (every number and statement backed by an anchor); METHODS §4.5, §6.2
findings.issue: Only the 11 h figure is anchored (Kish, 2008, second-hand). The '10' in 'roughly 10–11 hours' comes from the unread Cruickshank card, whose anchor is a placeholder, and the onset-by-route sentence has no anchor at all. The clause 'the felt effects do not last as long (see the time-course claim)' cites a claim that reports only times of peak: Hart et al. followed ratings for 4 h, and at 24 h Kirkpatrick et al. still found lower 'content' after the larger dose.
findings.evidence: evidence[0] (cruickshank_2009: page, locator and extracted are placeholders); evidence[1] (about 11 h, cited by the author to a review); sc_cruickshank_2009 analysis.effect_sizes ('about 10 h', marked to be extracted from the PDF); sc_hart_2008 design_detail (ratings to 4 h); sc_kirkpatrick_2012 key_findings[10] (24-h 'content' 40.7 vs 54.6 after 50 mg/70 kg vs placebo).
findings.proposed: Statement: "In adults, methamphetamine's plasma elimination half-life is about 11 hours after smoked, intranasal or intravenous use, a figure cited second-hand in a narrative review (Kish, 2008); the primary pharmacokinetic studies have not yet been read. At that rate about a quarter of the peak plasma level would remain about 22 hours after the peak (editors' calculation)." Delete the onset sentence and the felt-effects clause until they are anchored to primary studies. Magnitude: "t½ about 11 h for smoked, intranasal and intravenous use (Kish, 2008, citing a review). Range, onset and bioavailability by route: not yet extracted."

findings.rule: Brief B; factual accuracy
findings.issue: 'About half of a dose is still in the blood 10–11 hours later' misdefines half-life: it is the time for the blood level to halve after the peak, and after a snorted dose the level is still rising at 3–4 hours. 'Well after the felt effects have faded' has no anchor (see the statement finding).
findings.evidence: cl_meth_pk_intranasal_timecourse evidence[0] and [2] (plasma highest at the 3–4 h samples); sc_hart_2008 design_detail (subjective ratings measured to 4 h only).
findings.proposed: "Meth is cleared from the blood slowly. Once the level in the blood has peaked, it takes about 11 hours to fall by half. This figure comes from a review; the original studies still need to be checked."

findings.rule: METHODS §6.4; review brief D
findings.issue: 'Replicated' needs at least two independent studies in the same direction. The only located evidence is one second-hand figure in a narrative review (AMSTAR 2 critically low), and the second anchor is an unfilled placeholder.
findings.evidence: evidence[0]–[1]; sc_kish_2008 risk_of_bias.overall (critically low); evidence[1].extracted (figure cited to a review, not a primary study).
findings.proposed: Status "single-study" until at least two primary pharmacokinetic studies from different groups are read and anchored (candidates: the controlled intranasal study by Harris et al., 2003, cited in Hart et al., 2008, and the primary sources behind cruickshank_2009). Revisit 'replicated' then.

findings.rule: GRADE; METHODS §6.3 (weakest necessary link)
findings.issue: Certainty 'moderate' rests on one second-hand statement in a critically low-confidence narrative review, and the reasoning itself says the primary studies must be cited before publication. A single downgrade for indirectness leaves the rating higher than the located evidence supports.
findings.evidence: grade.reasoning; sc_kish_2008 risk_of_bias (critically low); evidence[1].
findings.proposed: Leave the claim unrated while it is a draft, or rate it: starting_level high; risk_of_bias 1; indirectness 1; certainty low. Reasoning: "Controlled pharmacokinetic studies would start high, but none has been read. The only located figure is cited second-hand in a narrative review (AMSTAR 2 critically low) and cannot be traced to its primary data (−1 risk of bias; −1 indirectness). Rated low until the primary studies are read and anchored."

findings.rule: METHODS §6.3 (overlapping evidence: one laboratory's successive studies) and §6.4; review brief D
findings.issue: The status is 'replicated', but both studies come from one laboratory (same NIDA grant, same institute), which §6.3 does not count as independent replication. The grade reasoning itself says so.
findings.evidence: grade.reasoning ('Both studies come from the same laboratory'); sc_kirkpatrick_2012 funding (DA-19559 to Dr Hart) and replication.where_it_stands; sc_hart_2008 replication.where_it_stands.
findings.proposed: Status "single-study". Add to the statement: "Both studies come from one laboratory, so they are not independent replications."

findings.rule: Brief A (statement says no more than the anchors)
findings.issue: The 15-minute subjective peak is attributed to both studies, but only Hart et al. (2008) timed subjective effects; Kirkpatrick et al. analysed ratings as session totals, and their anchor gives cardiovascular timing only. 'Peaked about 3–4 hours' is also bounded by sampling: Kirkpatrick's last plasma sample was at 4 h, and Hart's next sample after 4 h was at 6 h.
findings.evidence: evidence[2] (Kirkpatrick: cardiovascular timing only); sc_kirkpatrick_2012 exposure.measurement (plasma at baseline, 15, 60, 90, 120, 180, 240 min) and outcomes.instruments (ratings summed over the session); sc_hart_2008 key_findings[2] note (peak bounded by the sampling schedule).
findings.proposed: Replace "plasma methamphetamine peaked about 3–4 hours after dosing, whereas the rises in heart rate, blood pressure and subjective effects peaked within about 15 minutes" with "plasma methamphetamine was highest at the 3–4-hour samples (the last sample taken in one study and the last before 6 hours in the other, so the true peak may be later), whereas heart rate and blood pressure peaked within about 15 minutes in both studies, and subjective ratings at 15 minutes in the one study that reported their timing".

findings.rule: Brief B (plain means the same as the statement); METHODS §8 (template section)
findings.issue: The plain drops the population (people who use regularly, single doses) and the whole next-day heart-rate finding, so it does not say what the statement says. The next-day finding is a physiological effect, not pharmacokinetics, and would sit better in section 5.
findings.evidence: statement vs plain; METHODS §8 (section 5: physiological effects in controlled studies).
findings.proposed: Either move the next-day heart-rate sentence and its anchors (evidence[3]–[5]) to cl_meth_acute_lab, or use this plain: "In lab studies, adults who use meth regularly were given single snorted doses. Heart rate and blood pressure peaked within about 15 minutes, and so did the felt effects in the study that timed them, while the amount of drug in the blood was still rising 3–4 hours later. In one study, heart rate the next morning was about 9–11 beats a minute higher than after a dummy dose, but this may have come from drug use outside the lab."

findings.rule: METHODS §6.3 (editors' calculations are labelled)
findings.issue: '9–11 beats per minute' is a difference the editors computed from the printed means (86.1−76.8 and 87.8−76.8) but is not labelled as such.
findings.evidence: evidence[3].extracted.
findings.proposed: "9–11 beats per minute higher (editors' calculation from the printed means)".

findings.rule: Brief C (reasoning matches the domain levels)
findings.issue: Risk of bias is set at 0 without saying why, although Kirkpatrick et al. are rated RoB 2 'high' for carryover, blinding and selective reporting. The reasoning also calls both studies randomized, but Hart et al. counterbalanced dose order without randomizing it.
findings.evidence: sc_kirkpatrick_2012 risk_of_bias; sc_hart_2008 risk_of_bias, domain 1.
findings.proposed: First sentence: "Placebo-controlled within-subject studies (dose order randomized in one, counterbalanced in the other) start high." Add: "Risk of bias is not downgraded for the timing outcomes, which are assayed or automated. The RoB 2 concerns (high in Kirkpatrick et al. for carryover, blinding and selective reporting) bear on the ratings and on the next-day values, which are reported here as uncertain."

findings.rule: Brief A (a number that does not match its anchor)
findings.issue: The 10% lower bound comes from Hart et al.'s description of Johanson et al. (2006): DAT and VMAT2 binding 10–16% lower, a single range for two markers. Kish et al. put that study's VMAT2 reduction at about 10%, so the 10% may not be a DAT figure at all.
findings.evidence: evidence[8].extracted (DAT and VMAT2 together); Hart_2012 page text, PDF page 11 = p. 596, 2nd paragraph; cl_meth_vmat2 evidence[5] (Kish: VMAT2 about 10% lower in that study).
findings.proposed: Statement: replace "about 10–28% lower in individual PET studies" with "about 13–28% lower in individual PET studies (a further study reports DAT and VMAT2 together as 10–16% lower)". Magnitude: replace "13–23% and 10–16% in two further studies as described by Hart et al. (2012)" with "13–23% (McCann et al., 2008) and, for DAT and VMAT2 together, 10–16% (Johanson et al., 2006), both as described by Hart et al. (2012)". Plain: replace "about a tenth to a quarter less" with "about 13–28% less". Alternative if a DAT-only range that includes Johanson et al. is wanted: London et al. (2015) give 11–28% across six PET studies (sc_london_2015 key_findings[6]); add that anchor.

findings.rule: Brief A
findings.issue: 'About −19% with the authors' age correction' appears in no anchor's extracted text; the age-corrected values are on the card only.
findings.evidence: evidence[4].extracted (no age-corrected values); sc_mccann_1998 key_findings[4] (age-corrected caudate 7.0 vs 8.7 and putamen 6.7 vs 8.3; Table 3 and legend).
findings.proposed: Add to evidence[4].extracted: "With the authors' fixed age correction (0.8% per year): caudate 7.0 vs 8.7 and putamen 6.7 vs 8.3, about 19% lower in both (Table 3 and legend)." Magnitude: "about −19% in both regions with the authors' fixed age correction".

findings.rule: METHODS §6.3 (rate the claim as worded; downgrade when remaining biases could change the estimate materially); brief C
findings.issue: Risk of bias is not downgraded although every primary card is ROBINS-E high or very high (unadjusted comparisons, treatment-centre users against advertisement-recruited controls, unmatched smoking and sex, unmeasured other drug use), and the claim states sizes (13–28%; g −1.47). The reasoning concedes the size is less certain than the direction, but the rating does not reflect that.
findings.evidence: sc_volkow_2001a risk_of_bias (confounding high, selection high); sc_mccann_1998 (high); sc_volkow_2001b (very high); sc_ashok_2017 (AMSTAR 2 critically low); grade.reasoning, last sentence.
findings.proposed: Preferred: keep certainty low for the direction and say in the statement that the size is less certain. Add to the statement: "The direction is consistent across research groups; the size is uncertain." Add to the reasoning: "Rated for the direction. The size of the difference is very low certainty: every primary study is an unadjusted comparison of treatment-programme users with advertisement-recruited controls, with imbalances in smoking and sex where these were reported and unmeasured other drug use, and the pooled estimate comes from a critically low-confidence meta-analysis." Alternative if the magnitudes stay in the rated claim: risk_of_bias 1, certainty very-low, with the same reasoning.

findings.rule: METHODS §6.3 (overlapping evidence; weakest necessary link); brief A
findings.issue: The pooled g −1.47 is given without saying that the meta-analysis is critically low confidence, ran no analysis by abstinence, smoking or other drug use, and includes two studies each from the Volkow and McCann groups whose samples may overlap (Volkow 2001a and 2001b share 12 users). Overlap would make the interval too narrow.
findings.evidence: sc_ashok_2017 risk_of_bias.overall and sample.selection_effects; sc_volkow_2001b reporting_issues[6].
findings.proposed: After "(108 users, 126 controls; one study was of dexamphetamine users)" insert "; the meta-analysis is rated critically low confidence and includes two studies each from two research groups whose samples may overlap, so its interval is probably too narrow".

findings.rule: Brief B; brief E
findings.issue: 'Many individual users are in the normal range' is stronger than the anchors ('several users', 'considerable overlap'). The plain also omits that users smoked tobacco and used other drugs more often than the comparison groups.
findings.evidence: evidence[1], evidence[9]; sc_volkow_2001a sample.selection_effects (smokers 73% vs 24% in the companion paper).
findings.proposed: "On brain scans, people who used meth heavily and then stopped have on average about 13–28% less of the dopamine transporter (the protein that clears dopamine after it is released) in the striatum than people who don't use. Some users' values fall within the range of people who don't use. The users also smoked tobacco and used other drugs more often. The scans can't tell whether the difference means damaged nerve endings, the brain making less of the protein, or a difference that was there before use."

findings.rule: Brief F (same fact given with different numbers); internal consistency
findings.issue: The short-abstinence difference is 'about 21–25%' in the statement, '26% and 21%' in the magnitude, and 26%/21% in cl_meth_dat_lower. The card advises using the table-derived 25% for the caudate, because the text's 26% cannot be obtained from the table.
findings.evidence: evidence[1].extracted; sc_volkow_2001b reporting_issues[5]; Volkow 2001b PDF page 3 = p. 9416, Table 1 (1.32 vs 1.76; 1.56 vs 1.97).
findings.proposed: Statement: "were about 21–25% lower" → "were about 25% (caudate) and 21% (putamen) lower". Magnitude: "short abstinence 26% and 21% below" → "short abstinence 25% (caudate; 26% in the text) and 21% (putamen) below". Use the same figures in cl_meth_dat_lower evidence[3].

findings.rule: Brief A (selective use of sources) and E
findings.issue: The statement cites one PET study with no relation between abstinence and DAT. But the programme's own baseline analysis found none either (r<0.11, with the authors inferring no significant recovery within a year), and so did Johanson et al. (2006). The statement also leaves out the only DAT follow-up with retested controls (Chou et al., 2007), which found a rise, though from a first scan taken while urine tests were still positive.
findings.evidence: Volkow_2001a page text, PDF page 3 = p. 379 (r<0.11, df=14, p>0.70) and PDF page 5 = p. 381 (no significant recovery after 1 year); Hart_2012 PDF page 11 = p. 596 (Johanson et al.: imaging not correlated with abstinence duration); Dean_2013 PDF page 7 = p. 265 (Chou et al.: 5 users, mean +20% over 2 weeks; 7 controls −14% to +13%; first scan urine-positive).
findings.proposed: Replace "and another PET study found no relation between abstinence duration and transporter levels" with "and three cross-sectional analyses, including this programme's own baseline study, found no relation between time since last use and transporter levels (Volkow et al., 2001a; Johanson et al., 2006, and McCann et al., 2008, as described by Hart et al., 2012). The one DAT follow-up with retested controls (5 users, 7 controls, SPECT) reported a mean 20% rise over 2 weeks, but its first scan was taken while urine tests were still positive (Chou et al., 2007, as described by Dean et al., 2013)." Add anchors: volkow_2001a p. 379 (role contradicts) and dean_2013 p. 265 (role qualifies).

findings.rule: METHODS §6.3 (absence of evidence needs precision)
findings.issue: 'A moderate remaining difference is not excluded' understates the imprecision. The 95% intervals reach −1.2 (caudate) and −1.5 (putamen), about the size of the short-abstinence difference (g about −1.5).
findings.evidence: This review's recomputation from Volkow 2001b Table 1 (p. 9416), Hedges' g with pooled SD: protracted vs controls −0.31 (95% CI −1.17 to 0.55) caudate and −0.57 (−1.45 to 0.30) putamen; short abstinence vs controls −1.54 and −1.51.
findings.proposed: Replace "(n=10 vs 11; editors' standardized difference about −0.3 and −0.6, so a moderate remaining difference is not excluded)" with "(n=10 vs 11; editors' calculation: g −0.3, 95% CI −1.2 to 0.6, and −0.6, −1.5 to 0.3, so a remaining difference about as large as in short abstinence, g about −1.5, is not excluded)".

findings.rule: Brief B (stronger wording than the statement)
findings.issue: 'Close to the levels of people who don't use' asserts a return to normal that a 10-versus-11 comparison with wide intervals cannot show. 'Another study did not find this pattern' understates the contrary evidence.
findings.evidence: magnitude; evidence[1]; finding above on omitted null correlations.
findings.proposed: "Five people from a court-supervised treatment programme were scanned twice. After more than a year without meth, their dopamine transporter levels had risen by about a sixth to a fifth. A group scanned after more than a year without meth was not clearly different from people who don't use, but the groups were too small to rule out a large difference. Studies comparing people with shorter and longer time since last use found no such pattern. Five people is too few to know how typical this is, and those who stayed abstinent had higher levels to begin with."

findings.rule: METHODS §9 (dependence and use disorder in their DSM-5/ICD-11 senses, with the instrument named)
findings.issue: 'Use disorder' is applied to samples diagnosed with DSM-IV methamphetamine dependence. The statement also says 'treatment programme' where the drug-court setting (relapse meant jail) is part of the selection.
findings.evidence: Volkow_2001b PDF page 2 = p. 9415 (DSM-IV dependence; California drug-court monitoring programme); Wang_2004 PDF pages 2 and 6 = pp. 243, 247.
findings.proposed: Population (both claims): "Adults with DSM-IV methamphetamine dependence in a court-supervised treatment programme (relapse meant a return to jail)". Statement: "from a treatment programme" → "from a court-supervised treatment programme".

findings.rule: Brief B (qualifiers dropped)
findings.issue: 'Higher than normal in the first days after use and back to normal after about 10 days' drops 'on average' and 'in those who stayed abstinent', who had been less raised to begin with. The 10-day comparison (17 vs 9) could not show a return to normal, and the within-person fall was not significant (p=0.055).
findings.evidence: evidence[1], evidence[3]; sc_boileau_2016 key_findings[5] (11% fall, p=0.055; individual changes −34% to +29%).
findings.proposed: "Another dopamine marker, VMAT2 (the protein that packs dopamine into storage vesicles), gave a higher scan signal on average in people scanned a few days after last using meth. In those who then stayed off meth for about 10 days, who had been less raised to begin with, it no longer differed clearly from a small comparison group. The researchers think the raised signal reflects low stored dopamine rather than more of the protein, which the study could not test. After long abstinence, studies disagree on whether it ends up slightly lower."

findings.rule: Brief A and E (a PDF-read source settles the discrepancy; size understated)
findings.issue: The statement reports the long-abstinence study's abstinence as inconsistent between reviews (3 months vs 3 years). But Hart et al.'s Table 2 settles it: a required minimum of 3 months, a mean of 3.4 years and a range to 18 years. The statement also gives only '10% lower' although the meta-analysis expresses that difference as a large standardized one (g 1.68), and it omits the second post-mortem study's non-significant trend lower.
findings.evidence: Hart_2012 page text, PDF page 8 = p. 593, Table 2 (Johanson et al., 2006 row); evidence[5] (Kish); evidence[6] (Ashok, g 1.68); sc_kish_2017 key_findings[4].
findings.proposed: Replace the last sentence with: "A review reports post-mortem VMAT2 in users as normal in one study (a second showed a non-significant trend lower). One PET study of users abstinent a mean of 3.4 years (minimum 3 months; Hart et al., 2012, Table 2) found binding about 10% lower, which a meta-analysis expresses as a large standardized difference (g 1.68)." Add an anchor: hart_2012, p. 593, Table 2 (Johanson et al., 2006 row).

findings.rule: METHODS §6.3–6.4; review brief D
findings.issue: 'Mixed' means inconsistent findings without an adequate explanation. But the claim's main finding, raised binding in early abstinence, comes from one laboratory's two studies with partly shared controls, and the claim itself explains the early-versus-late difference by time since last use.
findings.evidence: sc_boileau_2016 replication.where_it_stands (twice, same laboratory, partly shared controls); sc_ashok_2017 exposure.abstinence_at_testing (VMAT2 studies at 2.6 and 19 days); statement.
findings.proposed: Status "single-study". Add to the statement: "Raised binding in early abstinence has been reported by one laboratory only (two studies with partly shared controls)."

findings.rule: Internal consistency; METHODS §6.3 (editors' calculations recomputed)
findings.issue: Ashok et al.'s 'two early-abstinence studies, g 1.16 (0.56 to 1.76)' is identical to the editors' recomputed g for Boileau et al. (2016) alone. This suggests the meta-analysis printed one study's estimate as a two-study figure. Separately, sc_boileau_2016 still shows the superseded 1.24 (0.63–1.85).
findings.evidence: magnitude (editors' g 1.16, 0.56–1.76); sc_ashok_2017 key_findings[4]; sc_boileau_2016 key_findings[2]; this review's recomputation from Table 3 (pooled SD): g 1.16 (0.56 to 1.76).
findings.proposed: Add to evidence[6].extracted: "(the printed g and interval equal the single-study value for Boileau et al., 2016; whether two studies were pooled is not stated)". Update sc_boileau_2016 key_findings[2] and analysis.effect_sizes to whole-striatum g 1.16 (0.56 to 1.76) (editors' recomputation).

findings.rule: Brief A
findings.issue: 'Tracked recency and amount of use' rests partly on a monthly-amount variable that the card flags as internally inconsistent (0.35 g/day on about 17 days a month against 1.57 g a month).
findings.evidence: sc_boileau_2016 reporting_issues[1]; evidence[2].
findings.proposed: "tracked how recently and how often methamphetamine had been used (the amount variable is internally inconsistent)".

findings.rule: Brief A (numbers not in any anchor)
findings.issue: 'In absolute terms caudate metabolism was about equal to controls' and putamen about 8% higher' appears in no anchor. It is the second reader's reading of Figure 2, recorded only on the card, which also gives the thalamus as about 4% lower in absolute terms.
findings.evidence: evidence[0]–[5]; sc_volkow_2001c key_findings[6] (Figure 2, p. 385); arithmetic from the printed relative and global percentages gives about −5%, +1% and +7%, consistent with the reading.
findings.proposed: Add an anchor: {reference volkow_2001c; page 'p. 385'; locator 'Figure 2 (editors' reading of the bars)'; extracted 'Absolute regional metabolism, users vs controls (editors' reading of Figure 2): thalamus about 4% lower, caudate about equal, putamen about 8% higher; consistent with the printed relative differences divided by a 14% higher global value.'; role qualifies}. Statement: replace "in absolute terms caudate metabolism was about equal to controls' and putamen about 8% higher" with "in absolute terms (editors' reading of a figure) thalamic metabolism was about 4% lower, caudate about equal and putamen about 8% higher".

findings.rule: Brief A and E; METHODS §6.4 (mixed = heterogeneity without adequate explanation)
findings.issue: The non-replication is given without the difference in abstinence (London et al.: 4–7 days; this study: 2 weeks to 35 months). It also omits the same group's later comparison of 12 of the same users with other controls, where the 14% excess was not significant, and a control-retested study suggesting that global metabolism rises over the first month. Separately, the population field says 'days to months' for abstinence of 2 weeks to 35 months.
findings.evidence: Volkow_2001c PDF page 2 = p. 384 (12 tested 2 weeks–5 months after last use, 3 at 11–35 months); Hart_2012 PDF page 9 = p. 594, Table 2 (London et al., 2004: 4–7 days); Wang_2004 PDF page 3 = p. 244 (38.5 vs 33.8 µmol/100 g/min, not significant); Dean_2013 PDF page 7 = p. 265 (Berman et al., 2007); sc_wang_2004 key_findings[6].
findings.proposed: Replace "Another research group found no difference in global metabolism." with "Another research group, studying people 4–7 days after last use, found no difference in global metabolism. The same research group, comparing 12 of the same users with a different control group, found a similar 14% excess that was not significant (Wang et al., 2004). In a study that retested controls, global metabolism rose more in users than in controls over the first month of abstinence (Berman et al., 2007, as described by Dean et al., 2013), so timing may explain part of the disagreement." Population: "Adults with heavy methamphetamine use, abstinent 2 weeks to 35 months (12 of 15 within 5 months)". Add anchors: wang_2004 p. 244; hart_2012 p. 594 (Table 2); dean_2013 p. 265.

findings.rule: Brief B (a qualifier that changes the meaning is dropped)
findings.issue: The plain says the study 'found more activity overall' without the qualifier, kept in the statement, that the difference did not meet the study's own threshold for significance.
findings.evidence: evidence[2] (threshold p<0.01; global difference p<0.05).
findings.proposed: "One brain-energy study found more activity overall in people who had stopped meth, but the difference did not meet the study's own standard for significance. Deep brain structures looked lower only when compared with that higher overall level. Another group, studying people who had stopped more recently, did not find the overall difference. The groups also differed in smoking and in the share of women, so these scans can't show what meth did."

findings.rule: METHODS §4.5 (page locator)
findings.issue: Figure 2 is on p. 385, as the card was corrected, but the anchor still reads p. 384.
findings.evidence: Volkow_2001c page text: the Figure 2 caption is on PDF page 3 = p. 385; sc_volkow_2001c verification.disagreements[0].
findings.proposed: page "pp. 384–385"; locator "Results, 1st paragraph (p. 384); Figure 2 (p. 385)".

findings.rule: Brief A; METHODS §6.3 (editors' calculations labelled)
findings.issue: 'Global metabolism (about −4%)' is an unlabelled editors' calculation from 42.6 vs 40.8 µmol/100 g/min. 'Absolute thalamic metabolism ... did not change significantly' is not in the anchor either; both appear only on p. 244 and on the card.
findings.evidence: Wang_2004 PDF page 3 = p. 244 (Results, 1st paragraph: global 42.6 vs 40.8; no differences in absolute striatal, thalamic or occipital measures); sc_wang_2004 key_findings[0].
findings.proposed: Add to evidence[0].extracted: "Global metabolism 42.6 (SD 4.0) vs 40.8 (SD 3.4) µmol/100 g/min (editors' calculation: about −4%); absolute striatal, thalamic and occipital metabolism did not differ between scans." Statement: "global metabolism (about −4%)" → "global metabolism (about −4%, editors' calculation)".

findings.rule: Brief A (qualifying findings in the same source left out)
findings.issue: 'Relative striatal metabolism remained lower than in controls' omits two qualifiers from the same paper. In absolute values, the voxelwise analysis found no group differences. And the authors say that users' higher whole-brain metabolism could contribute to the lower relative striatal values.
findings.evidence: Wang_2004 PDF page 3 = p. 244 (statistical parametric mapping of absolute values: no differences between groups); PDF page 6 = p. 247 (Limitations, 2nd point).
findings.proposed: Replace "relative striatal metabolism remained lower than in controls" with "relative striatal metabolism remained lower than in controls, although in absolute values no group difference was found and the authors note that a higher whole-brain value in users could contribute to the lower relative values". Add anchors: wang_2004 p. 244 and p. 247 (role qualifies).

findings.rule: METHODS §6.3 (overlapping evidence: the claim says so); brief F
findings.issue: 'The same treatment programme' has no antecedent in a standalone claim. Neither the statement nor the reasoning says these are the same five people whose DAT rose in cl_meth_dat_recovery, so the two recovery claims are one small follow-up, not two pieces of evidence.
findings.evidence: Wang_2004 PDF page 2 = p. 243 (the five come from the original 12 and stayed drug-free; same drug-court programme); sc_wang_2004 replication.timeline (DAT follow-up of the same 5).
findings.proposed: Statement: "In five people from the same treatment programme rescanned after 12–17 months of abstinence" → "In the same five people whose dopamine transporter levels were followed in cl_meth_dat_recovery (a court-supervised treatment programme), rescanned after 12–17 months of abstinence". Plain: add "These are the same five people as in the dopamine transporter follow-up." Reasoning: add "Same participants as cl_meth_dat_recovery; not independent evidence of recovery."

findings.rule: METHODS §4.5 (an anchor states what the source says)
findings.issue: The Dean et al. anchor says pre–post studies cannot separate improvement 'from practice or retest effects', but the passage concerns practice effects on cognitive tests. Dean et al. do not raise retest artefacts for FDG-PET, and on p. 265 they judge a pure retest artefact unlikely for the DAT increase.
findings.evidence: Dean_2013 PDF pages 5–6 = pp. 263–264 (Hypothesis 4: practice effects on test scores); PDF page 7 = p. 265 (DAT increase unlikely to be only a retest artefact; for Wang et al., no control of practice effects on retesting).
findings.proposed: "Dean et al. note that pre–post studies without retested controls, including Wang et al. (2004), cannot separate cognitive improvement from practice effects on the tests; they do not discuss test–retest variation of the PET measure." Keep 'No control group was rescanned' in the statement, anchored to Wang 2004 p. 243.

findings.rule: METHODS §6.3; brief B (short sentences)
findings.issue: For protracted abstinence, the thalamic value 'reported as not different' (1.23 vs 1.31) hides a sizeable standardized difference that is on the card. Separately, the plain's last sentence is a fragment.
findings.evidence: sc_wang_2004 key_findings[2] note (d about −0.8, p about 0.05–0.07); this review's recomputation: g −0.8 (95% CI −1.7 to 0.1).
findings.proposed: Magnitude: "1.23 vs 1.31 (protracted; reported as not different; editors' calculation d about −0.8, 95% CI −1.7 to 0.1)". Plain, last sentence: "This rests on five people, with no comparison group scanned twice, and the paper's statistics contain errors."

findings.rule: Brief E (stage of abstinence changes the reading)
findings.issue: Both studies scanned people in their first week of abstinence (Thompson: mean 6.6 days, self-reported; Morales: 4–7 days, urine-verified), and in Morales et al. grey matter rose over the following month. The statement says neither.
findings.evidence: sc_thompson_2004 exposure.abstinence_at_testing; sc_morales_2012 exposure.abstinence_at_testing and key_findings[5]; evidence[5].
findings.proposed: Insert after the first sentence: "Both studies scanned people in their first week without methamphetamine; in one, grey matter increased in several regions over the following month (at an uncorrected statistical threshold), so some differences may be temporary."

findings.rule: Brief A (statement says no more than the anchors)
findings.issue: The regions in the first sentence (frontal, cingulate, insular) come from the Morales comparison with non-smoking controls, but the anchor lists only the four clusters against smoking controls, so 'insular' is anchored nowhere. The sentence also says 'controls' where these differences were against non-smokers.
findings.evidence: evidence[3].extracted; sc_morales_2012 key_findings[1].
findings.proposed: Add to evidence[3].extracted: "Against non-smoking controls the ten clusters were right frontal pole/orbitofrontal, left orbitofrontal, left superior frontal, left insula, bilateral precentral, right middle temporal, right precuneus, left caudate and right cingulate (Table 2)." Statement: "than in controls" → "than in non-smoking controls".

findings.rule: Brief E (confounders the design cannot exclude)
findings.issue: The four clusters that remained against smoking controls are reported without the authors' sensitivity analysis: with education added, the results held only at an uncorrected threshold. The earlier study's groups also differed in education and depression scores, not only in smoking.
findings.evidence: sc_morales_2012 comparison.matching and reporting_issues[6]; evidence[2] (Thompson: education 12.8 vs 15.2 years, depression score 9.77 vs 1.25).
findings.proposed: After "mostly in places other than the 10 found against non-smoking controls" insert "; with education added to the model, the results held only at a more lenient uncorrected threshold". After "An earlier report of 7.8% smaller hippocampi" insert "(in groups that also differed in education, depression scores and smoking)".

findings.rule: METHODS §9 (no adjectives of reassurance; magnitudes are numbers); brief B
findings.issue: 'Slightly smaller' is an evaluative word where §9 asks for numbers. The plain also names only smoking, although the groups differed in schooling and depression and were scanned in the first week of abstinence.
findings.evidence: magnitude (11.3% density, 7.8% hippocampal volume); evidence[2]; sc_morales_2012 key_findings[5].
findings.proposed: "Brain scans taken in the first week after stopping showed some regions with less grey matter (differences of up to about 11% in one study), and a few larger, in people dependent on meth. Most of them also smoke tobacco, and in the study that checked, smokers who don't use meth showed some of the same differences. Users also had less schooling and more symptoms of depression. In one study, grey matter grew in several regions over the first month without meth. An early finding of a smaller memory region (the hippocampus) was not repeated by the same lab."

findings.rule: Brief A and F (contradicts its anchors and cl_meth_dat_lower); METHODS §7 (each side at its proponents' standard)
findings.issue: The 'yes' side says users were scanned after 'days to months' of abstinence and gives '20–28%'. But the cited studies include abstinence of up to 36 and 65 months, and cl_meth_dat_lower gives a different range. The box thereby omits the 'yes' side's strongest point: lower DAT was found after years of abstinence and was unrelated to time since last use.
findings.evidence: Volkow_2001a PDF page 2 = p. 378, Table 1 (abstinence 0.5–36 months) and PDF page 3 = p. 379 (no correlation with days since last use); sc_mccann_1998 key_findings[6] (about 4–65 months); Hart_2012 PDF page 8 = p. 593, Table 2 (McCann et al., 2008: imaging subset abstinent 77 ± 102 months, DAT 13–23% lower); cl_meth_dat_lower statement.
findings.proposed: Replace the first sentence with: "Heavy users scanned after days to years of abstinence have lower striatal dopamine transporter availability than non-users: about 13–28% lower in individual PET studies and g −1.47 pooled over 9 studies (Volkow et al., 2001a; McCann et al., 1998; Ashok et al., 2017). The difference was found in groups abstinent for years on average (nearly 3 years in McCann et al., 1998; about 6 years in McCann et al., 2008, as described by Hart et al., 2012), and three cross-sectional analyses found no relation with time since last use." Use the range finally adopted in cl_meth_dat_lower, and add the hart_2012 p. 593 anchor.

findings.rule: Brief A (generalization beyond the anchors)
findings.issue: 'Lower dopamine markers in heavy users are consistently found' overstates. Only the transporter is consistently lower. Low post-mortem dopamine comes from one laboratory's series in people who used within about 5 days of death, and VMAT2, dopamine metabolites and synthesizing enzymes are normal or raised.
findings.evidence: evidence[1]–[2]; sc_kish_2017 key_findings[2]–[4] and replication.where_it_stands; cl_meth_vmat2.
findings.proposed: Replace "lower dopamine markers in heavy users are consistently found" with "lower dopamine transporter levels in heavy users are consistently found, while markers such as VMAT2, dopamine metabolites and dopamine-synthesizing enzymes are normal or raised, and low post-mortem dopamine comes from one laboratory's series of people who used shortly before death".

findings.rule: METHODS §1.4 (symmetry) and §9; review standard (neither alarmist nor reassuring)
findings.issue: After the colon, the statement and plain list only reasons against damage and leave out the Parkinson's registry association, which the editors' reading calls the main reason the question stays open. Without it, 'the pattern doesn't look like Parkinson's disease' reads as reassurance.
findings.evidence: debate.editors_reading; evidence[14]–[15]; cl_meth_parkinson statement and magnitude.
findings.proposed: Statement: append "; two record-linkage studies found more later Parkinson's disease diagnoses after methamphetamine- or amphetamine-related diagnoses (in one, 0.30% vs 0.11% over about 7 years), though misclassified diagnoses are a plausible explanation (cl_meth_parkinson)". Plain: "Does meth damage dopamine nerve cells? Not shown either way. People who used meth heavily have less of one dopamine protein (the transporter), but this protein can drop without any nerve cells being lost, other markers of dopamine nerve endings are not lower, and in small studies the transporter rose again after people stopped. The pattern also differs from Parkinson's disease. On the other side, two record studies found Parkinson's diagnoses later on more often in people with meth-related diagnoses (about 3 versus 1 in 1,000 over 7 years in one), though some of those diagnoses may be wrong. See the contested question."

findings.rule: METHODS §7 (both sides written to the standard their best proponents would accept)
findings.issue: The 'yes' side leaves out three arguments its proponents draw from the cited studies. The DAT rise took longer than down-regulation would predict. In the same five people striatal metabolism did not recover, which the authors read as adaptation of surviving terminals. And the caudate–putamen pattern resembles atypical parkinsonism.
findings.evidence: Volkow_2001b PDF page 4 = p. 9417 (Interpretation of DAT losses, 2nd paragraph); Wang_2004 PDF page 4 = p. 245 (Discussion, 1st section); Volkow_2001c PDF page 5 = p. 387 (Discussion, 4th paragraph); sc_volkow_2001b key_findings[5] note; sc_volkow_2001c key_findings[7].
findings.proposed: Add to evidence_yes: "The authors of the follow-up argue that a recovery taking longer than 6–9 months is slower than down-regulation would produce (Volkow et al., 2001b). In the same five people striatal metabolism did not recover, which the group reads as adaptation of surviving terminals rather than reversal of damage (Wang et al., 2004). The same group likens the equal caudate and putamen transporter loss to atypical parkinsonism rather than Parkinson's disease (Volkow et al., 2001c)." Add the three anchors.

findings.rule: METHODS §6.3 (relative effects with absolute effects) and §7
findings.issue: The registry evidence is given without any numbers, and its limits appear nowhere in the box, although cl_meth_parkinson and the cards carry both.
findings.evidence: evidence[14]–[15]; sc_curtin_2015 key_findings[0], [6]–[8]; cl_meth_parkinson.
findings.proposed: evidence_yes, last sentence: "Two record-linkage cohorts found more later Parkinson's disease diagnoses after methamphetamine- or amphetamine-related diagnoses: in Utah HR 2.8 (95% CI 1.6–4.8; 0.30% vs 0.11% over a mean 6.8 years) and in California HR 1.76 (1.12–2.75), with no increase after cocaine-related diagnoses (Curtin et al., 2015; Kish et al., 2017)." neither_can_show, add: "Registry studies record diagnoses, not use or disease: in the Utah cohort the diagnoses came at a median age of 49, about 2 years after the first methamphetamine code, and few people received levodopa, so misclassified tremor or drug-induced parkinsonism cannot be excluded (Curtin et al., 2015)."

findings.rule: Brief F (consistency with cl_meth_vmat2) and A
findings.issue: Three sentences say more than their sources. VMAT2 is called normal after about 10 days, though only the 17 who stayed abstinent were rescanned (against 9 controls) and their fall was not significant. 'Caudate more than putamen' describes post-mortem dopamine, whereas transporter loss on PET was similar in both. And escalating pre-exposure prevented binge effects only in a few rat studies, while escalating regimens in monkeys still lowered DAT and D2.
findings.evidence: cl_meth_vmat2 statement; sc_boileau_2016 key_findings[5]–[6]; Volkow_2001a PDF page 4 = p. 380; sc_mccann_1998 key_findings[0] (caudate 23%, putamen 25%); sc_dean_2013 key_findings[0]; evidence[13] (London 2015).
findings.proposed: Replace "The vesicular transporter, a marker of terminal integrity, was raised in the first days after use and normal after about 10 days (Boileau et al., 2016)." with "Binding to the vesicular transporter, a marker used for terminal integrity, was raised rather than lowered in the first days after use, and in the 17 people who stayed abstinent for about 10 days it no longer differed clearly from 9 rescanned controls (Boileau et al., 2016)." Replace "The pattern of loss (caudate more than putamen) is the reverse of Parkinson's disease" with "Post-mortem dopamine loss was greater in the caudate than the putamen, and transporter loss on PET was similar in both, unlike Parkinson's disease, in which the putamen is most affected". Replace "and escalating pre-exposure can prevent it (Hart et al., 2012)" with "and in a few rat studies escalating pre-exposure prevented the effects of a later binge (Hart et al., 2012; Dean et al., 2013)".

findings.rule: METHODS §7 (the reading gives its certainty and reasoning); brief F
findings.issue: 'Part of the change appears to reverse with abstinence' rests on cl_meth_dat_recovery (five selected people, very low certainty, status mixed) without saying so. The reading also repeats the statement's overgeneralization that lower dopamine markers are well replicated.
findings.evidence: cl_meth_dat_recovery grade and status; sc_kish_2017 replication.where_it_stands.
findings.proposed: "Editors' reading (certainty: very low). Lower striatal dopamine transporter levels in heavy users are well replicated; markers such as VMAT2, dopamine metabolites and synthesizing enzymes are normal or raised, and loss of dopamine neurons in humans has not been demonstrated. Whether the transporter difference reverses with abstinence is uncertain: one follow-up of five selected people found a rise, while cross-sectional studies found no relation with time since last use. The Parkinson's-disease registry signal, which may partly reflect misclassified diagnoses, is the main reason the question cannot be closed in either direction."

findings.rule: METHODS §2.3 (primary studies) and §6.3
findings.issue: The 50–61% post-mortem dopamine figure is cited to a review. It is one laboratory's series of 20 people who had used within about 5 days of death and has not been independently replicated.
findings.evidence: evidence[1]; sc_kish_2017 key_findings[1] and replication.where_it_stands.
findings.proposed: "Post-mortem, striatal dopamine was 50–61% lower in 20 users who had used within about 5 days of death, in one laboratory's series not yet independently replicated (as described by Kish et al., 2017)."

findings.rule: METHODS §6.3 (overlapping evidence) and §6.4; review brief D
findings.issue: 'Replicated' rests on two studies from one laboratory (same NIDA grant, same institute), which §6.3 does not count as independent. No study from another group is anchored.
findings.evidence: evidence[0]–[3]; sc_kirkpatrick_2012 funding and replication.where_it_stands; sc_hart_2008 replication.where_it_stands (a single-laboratory study).
findings.proposed: Status "single-study"; add to the statement: "Both studies come from one laboratory." Keep 'replicated' only after anchoring an independent laboratory's controlled study (for example Harris et al., 2003, cited in Hart et al., 2008, which had no placebo arm). The at-a-glance list can keep this claim for its certainty but should not present it as replicated.

findings.rule: Brief C (reasoning matches the domain levels); METHODS §5.3
findings.issue: The risk-of-bias downgrade is justified by reporting errors and missing statistics, which bear on precision and reporting rather than bias. The domain judgments that matter are blinding (every participant had received the top dose openly before the study; Kirkpatrick: high), carryover (Kirkpatrick: high) and selection of the reported result (Kirkpatrick: high). The reasoning also calls both studies randomized, but Hart et al. counterbalanced dose order.
findings.evidence: sc_hart_2008 risk_of_bias; sc_kirkpatrick_2012 risk_of_bias.
findings.proposed: "Placebo-controlled within-subject studies (dose order randomized in one, counterbalanced in the other) start high. Risk of bias (−1): RoB 2 some concerns (Hart et al., 2008) and high (Kirkpatrick et al., 2012), mainly because every participant had received the largest dose openly before the study and blinding was not checked (subjective ratings), carryover was possible (24-hour residual effects), and only significant rating items were tabulated. The cardiovascular and plasma measures are automated or assayed and the effects are large, so one level. Not downgraded for indirectness because the claim is restricted to single intranasal doses in experienced users; both studies come from one laboratory."

findings.rule: Brief E (selective reporting); review standard
findings.issue: Both papers tabulated only items that changed significantly. Ratings such as anxious, paranoid and bad drug effect (Hart et al.) and the questionnaire's 'bad effects' item (Kirkpatrick et al.) were collected but not reported, so the statement's list of effects cannot show that these did not occur.
findings.evidence: sc_hart_2008 analysis.selective_reporting; sc_kirkpatrick_2012 reporting_issues[4].
findings.proposed: Append to the statement: "Both studies tabulated only items that changed significantly; ratings such as anxious, paranoid or bad drug effect were collected but not reported, so their absence is not shown."

findings.rule: METHODS §9 (magnitudes are numbers); brief B
findings.issue: 'At the largest dose people also felt jittery and sweaty' gives no size (mean ratings about 25–43 of 100, against 2–11 after placebo) and implies these effects occurred only at the largest dose.
findings.evidence: evidence[2]; sc_hart_2008 key_findings[6].
findings.proposed: "In controlled lab studies, a single snorted dose raised heart rate and blood pressure and made people feel good, high and stimulated, more so at larger doses. Ratings of feeling jittery, sweaty and of a racing heart also rose, most at the largest dose (to about 25–43 on a 0–100 scale, against 2–11 after a dummy dose). These were single doses in experienced users, not binges, and both studies came from one lab."

findings.rule: Brief A
findings.issue: 'Raised at all doses vs placebo' holds for Hart et al. only; Kirkpatrick et al. report significant cardiovascular rises for the 50 mg/70 kg conditions (study conditions).
findings.evidence: evidence[0], evidence[3].
findings.proposed: "Heart rate, systolic and diastolic pressure raised at all three doses vs placebo in one study and at the larger dose in the other (magnitudes in figures only)".

findings.rule: METHODS §1.4 (symmetry)
findings.issue: Both acute claims qualify laboratory doses only with the forensic comparison that places them at the low end of real-world exposure (Kish, 2008). The review they also cite states that most tested doses were in the range people use for euphoria. That view comes without data, but a reader should see it beside the other.
findings.evidence: Hart_2012 PDF page 7 = p. 592 and PDF page 19 = p. 604 (Conclusions, 1st paragraph); evidence[6] (Kish 2008).
findings.proposed: Add anchor {reference hart_2012; page 'p. 604'; locator 'Conclusions, 1st paragraph'; extracted 'The reviewers state that most laboratory doses were within the range used to produce euphoria outside the laboratory; no data are given.'; role qualifies}. Add to the statement: "Laboratory single doses produce lower blood levels than many forensic samples (Kish, 2008), though the review authors consider them within the range used recreationally."

findings.rule: Brief A (generalization beyond the population, dose and route studied); METHODS §9
findings.issue: The review's 16 studies are presented as reaching 'the same conclusion' for the claim's population. But 10 of the 16 gave oral doses, 11 were in people without a methamphetamine-use disorder or with histories not reported (one in drug-naive volunteers), and 7 came from the reviewers' own laboratory.
findings.evidence: Hart_2012 PDF pages 5–6 = pp. 590–591, Table 1 (participant and route columns); sc_hart_2012 sample.selection_effects (7 of 16 from the reviewers' laboratory).
findings.proposed: Replace "a review of 16 controlled dosing studies, nearly all of single doses, reached the same conclusion" with "a review of 16 controlled dosing studies, nearly all of single doses, found no worsening on any domain; 10 of them gave oral doses, 11 were in people without a methamphetamine-use disorder (or with histories not reported), and 7 came from the reviewers' own laboratory". Population: "Adults who used methamphetamine regularly and were not seeking treatment (the two studies read); the reviewed studies also include people with little or no stimulant experience".

findings.rule: Brief A (qualifying findings in the same sources left out)
findings.issue: Two qualifying findings in the anchors are left out. The digit-symbol improvement occurred in only one of the two studies. And in one reviewed study, d-methamphetamine was worse than placebo on a visuospatial task in the first session, which the review scored as no effect.
findings.evidence: evidence[1] (Kirkpatrick: no digit-symbol effect); evidence[2] (Silber et al., 2006); Hart_2012 PDF page 6 = p. 591, Table 1.
findings.proposed: Replace "(divided-attention tracking at all doses; digit-symbol substitution at the two smaller of three doses)" with "(divided-attention tracking at all doses in both studies; digit-symbol substitution at the two smaller of three doses in one study and not at all in the other)". After the review clause add ", although in one reviewed study d-methamphetamine was worse than placebo on a visuospatial task in the first session and better in the second, which the review scored as no effect".

findings.rule: METHODS §6.3 (no-detectable-effect claims need precision)
findings.issue: 'Too small to exclude small impairments' understates the imprecision: with 11 and 13 participants and no effect sizes, the card judges that small or moderate effects cannot be excluded. The no-worsening part is weaker than the improvement part and the reasoning should say so.
findings.evidence: sc_hart_2008 analysis.power; grade.reasoning.
findings.proposed: Statement: "The studies were too small to exclude small impairments" → "The studies were too small to exclude small or moderate impairments". Reasoning: add "The no-worsening part rests on non-significant results in 11 and 13 people and is very low certainty on its own; the improvement on divided attention is the better-supported part."

findings.rule: METHODS §6.3; brief B (stronger wording than the statement)
findings.issue: 'A single dose did not make people worse' asserts that there is no effect, while the statement and grade say impairments could not be excluded. The plain also drops the route and the population.
findings.evidence: statement; grade.reasoning.
findings.proposed: "In controlled lab studies, mostly of single doses, meth did not measurably worsen attention, memory or reaction-time tasks, and on some tasks people did better. The two main studies gave snorted doses to people who use meth regularly. The studies were small, so small or moderate harmful effects can't be ruled out, and binges or long-term use were not tested."

findings.rule: Brief B (clarity); internal consistency
findings.issue: 'In the same laboratory studies' has no antecedent in a standalone claim, and 'larger doses given repeatedly were not tested' repeats 'repeated or binge use was not tested'. The exposure field also omits the 40 mg oral maximum given in the anchor.
findings.evidence: evidence[2].extracted.
findings.proposed: Open with "In two double-blind, placebo-controlled laboratory studies from one research group (11 and 13 adults who used methamphetamine regularly and were not seeking treatment)," and end with "The studies were too small to exclude small or moderate impairments, and larger or repeated (binge) doses were not tested." Exposure: "up to 50 mg/70 kg intranasal, 30 mg intravenous or 40 mg oral in the reviewed studies (study conditions)".

findings.rule: METHODS §1.4 principle 2 (no text without a citable claim); §8 section 3
findings.issue: The mechanism line and the mechanism tags (VMAT2, TAAR1) are not supported by any claim. Section 3 has no claim on transporter or receptor pharmacology, TAAR1 appears in no card, and the only carded source says the mechanism is not completely understood.
findings.evidence: data/monographs/methamphetamine.json; sc_kish_2008 key_findings[0] (release by moving transmitter out of vesicles and reversing transport, described as apparent; mechanism not completely understood).
findings.proposed: Add a section-3 claim: "Methamphetamine raises extracellular dopamine, noradrenaline and serotonin by promoting their release from nerve endings, apparently by moving transmitter out of storage vesicles and reversing transport through the membrane transporters; the mechanism is not completely understood (Kish, 2008, narrative review; primary pharmacology to be cited)." Change the mechanism line to "A substituted amphetamine that releases dopamine, noradrenaline and serotonin from nerve endings, probably by reversing their transporters and releasing vesicular stores (section 3)." Remove "TAAR1" from mechanisms until a source is carded.

findings.rule: METHODS §8 (sections with no evidence say so)
findings.issue: Section 3 holds only the half-life draft and the intranasal time course. Metabolism and active metabolites, bioavailability by route, pharmacogenetics and interaction mechanisms are absent, with no note saying so.
findings.evidence: data/monographs/methamphetamine.json sections (number 3).
findings.proposed: Add no_evidence_note: "Not yet searched: metabolism and active metabolites, bioavailability by route, pharmacogenetics, mechanisms of drug–drug interactions."

needs_source_check.what: The PDF is in the project, but no page text reached this round. Extract the half-life range, onset and bioavailability by route, and the primary studies each rests on; the card's 'about 10 h' is unverified.
Confirm 'about 11 hours' for smoked, intranasal and intravenous use and the source it is cited to (PMC2413312, Introduction, 1st paragraph).
Whether subjective ratings were shown as a time course (Figure 3) with a 15-minute peak, and confirm that plasma sampling ended at 240 min (PMC3475187).
Figures 1–2 (images): plasma values at 4, 6, 12 and 24 h, and whether subjective ratings were back at placebo levels by 4 h. Needed before any claim on how long the felt effects last (PMC4918768).

Supplement: the 9 amphetamine-type DAT studies pooled. Check whether Volkow 2001a and 2001b (12 shared users) and both McCann studies are included, and how many were dexamphetamine studies (the card names Schrantee and Schouw; the claim says one).

needs_source_check.reference: Johanson et al. (2006), not in the project
needs_source_check.what: The DAT-specific percentage, separate from VMAT2, and the abstinence data. Needed for the lower bound of the PET range and for cl_meth_vmat2.

needs_source_check.reference: Chou et al. (2007); McCann et al. (2008), not in the project
needs_source_check.what: Primary papers for the control-retested SPECT follow-up and for the absence of a relation with abstinence; both now enter only through Dean et al. (2013) and Hart et al. (2012).

Whether 'g 1.16 (0.56 to 1.76)' for two early-abstinence studies is a pooled estimate or Boileau et al. (2016) alone, and the sign convention for VMAT2 effects (PMC5419581, Results, Other dopaminergic measures).
Which study is the second post-mortem VMAT2 study (non-significant trend lower) and in which regions (PMC5209286, VMAT2 section).

needs_source_check.reference: London et al. (2004); Berman et al. (2007), not in the project
needs_source_check.what: Primary papers for the non-replication of higher global metabolism (users 4–7 days abstinent) and for the control-retested change over the first month of abstinence.

Table 2 cluster locations against non-smoking controls (for the regions named in the statement), and whether the education sensitivity analysis covers the four clusters against smoking controls (PMC3427723).
Which studies report larger striatal and parietal volumes, and at what abstinence (Structural Brain Imaging, 2nd–3rd paragraphs; this is not among the card's key findings) (PMC4418947).
The PDF is in the project, but its card is a placeholder draft; the California HR 1.76 (1.12–2.75) enters only through Kish et al. (2017).
Whether the 12 mg/70 kg conditions (study conditions) raised heart rate or blood pressure above placebo; the text reports contrasts only for the 50 mg/70 kg conditions (PMC3475187).
Which of the 44 rating items were collected but not tabulated (anxious, paranoid, bad drug effect, confused), to word the selective-reporting caveat exactly (PMC4918768).

summary: The PDF anchors checked in this group (Volkow 2001a–c, Wang 2004, Dean 2013, Hart 2012) are on the pages they name, and their numbers match the page text. Most statements already carry the main design caveats: no pre-use scans, relative versus absolute metabolism, and selected completers. The main problems are at the level of protocol rules. 'Replicated' is given to two claims that rest on one laboratory's studies and to a half-life claim that rests on one second-hand figure with a placeholder anchor. Several statements carry numbers that no anchor contains: the 10 h half-life, the 10% DAT lower bound (which is a DAT-plus-VMAT2 figure), the age-corrected −19%, the absolute caudate and putamen metabolism, and the −4% global change. In the recovery claims, the plain language turns underpowered non-differences into 'back to normal' or 'close to' normal, three null abstinence correlations are left out, and two claims present the same five people as separate evidence. The dopamine-damage debate box misstates the abstinence of the 'yes' studies and omits that side's strongest points and the registry numbers and limits, while the statement lists only reasons against damage; the scepticism there needs to run both ways. Certainty ratings are mostly defensible, and no upgrades are used in this group. The exceptions are the half-life claim, which is rated too high for its evidence, and the DAT claim, which states magnitudes without the risk-of-bias downgrade its own reasoning implies.
